volumes.title: The Rope Hung Up
volumes.text:
For forty years I, Ansel Corrow, rang the tenor bell of Emberwick, and this autumn I hung up the rope. My ears are going. The doctor says, kindly, that the world will grow quieter for me each year, and that there is nothing to be done but get used to it.

I find I do not know what quiet is. I have spent my life making the opposite. A ringer thinks of quiet as the dull stretch between peals, as a baker thinks of an empty oven.

So I mean to study it, as one studies a new neighbour who is plainly going to stay. I shall go where quiet is kept, in houses and on the marsh and up the tower, and write down what I find. I confess I begin a little afraid of it. That seems worth writing down too.

volumes.title: The House After Guests
volumes.text:
My sister and her four grandchildren stayed a week and left this morning on the Lowlands coach. I, Ansel Corrow, who am making a study of quiet in my deaf old age, came back from the coach stop to my first specimen.

The house was quiet, but not as it had been quiet before they came. The chairs were still pulled out from the table. There was a wooden horse on the stairs and a damp towel on the banister. I stood in the hall and could very nearly hear them, the way you go on feeling a hat after you have taken it off.

So here is a first finding. Quiet is not empty. It keeps the shape of whatever has just left it, as a bed keeps the shape of the sleeper. I did not push the chairs in until supper.

volumes.title: Before Snow
volumes.text:
I walked out on the Fells road this afternoon under a sky the colour of pewter. I am Ansel Corrow, once bell-ringer of Emberwick, now a student of quiet, since quiet is coming for my ears whether I study it or not.

About three o'clock everything stopped. The rooks went down into the elms and said nothing. The wind dropped. A dog at the toll house, which barks at everybody, looked at me and did not bark. Even with good ears I think I should have heard nothing at all.

It did not feel like nothing. It felt like the moment when a ringer stands with the rope in both hands, before the first pull. Then the snow began, large flakes, in no hurry. Some quiet, I learned, is a kind of waiting, and the waiting is part of the thing waited for.

volumes.title: The Kettle Holds Its Breath
volumes.text:
Here is a thing I never noticed in seventy years of making tea. A kettle on the fire begins by ticking. Then it mutters, then it grumbles and roars. And then, just before it boils, it goes quiet.

I, Ansel Corrow, retired bell-ringer of Emberwick, noticed it only this winter, because my hearing is failing and I have taken to listening hard to the little that is left. I thought the fire had gone out. I bent down to look, and the lid began to dance.

So the kettle is quietest when it is nearest to its work. I have known ringers like that, and one cat. I had thought of quiet as what happens when nothing does. The kettle says otherwise. Some quiet is everything happening at once, under a lid. I drank the tea with respect.

volumes.title: The Wrong Sort
volumes.text:
I must set down, to be fair, that not all quiet is good. I, Ansel Corrow, have had three weeks of the wrong sort.

Hob Tansley and I rang side by side in the Emberwick tower for thirty years. At the mayor's daughter's wedding somebody came in a stroke late and spoiled the peal. I said it was Hob. Hob said it was me. Since then we have passed in the market like two carts in a narrow lane, each looking hard at the opposite hedge.

It is quiet between us, certainly. But it is the loudest quiet I ever sat in. I hear it through walls. The quiet before a snowfall is a breath drawn in. This is a breath held, and a held breath does nobody good for long. I note it here, and do not yet know what to do about it.

volumes.title: Forty People Reading
volumes.text:
On a wet Thursday I sat for two hours in the reading room of Emberwick Library. I had no book I wanted. I, Ansel Corrow, former bell-ringer, went to look at the quiet there, as part of my study of it.

There were perhaps forty of us. A schoolboy with an atlas. Two women sharing a book of gardens. The old corn merchant asleep behind a newspaper, which rose and fell. Nobody had ordered silence. Each person was simply keeping quiet for the sake of the others, and the others for them.

I had always thought quiet was something that happens to you. Here it was being made, by forty people at once, like a barn roof going up. When a page turned you could tell how carefully. I went home feeling I had been in good company, though nobody had said a word to me.

volumes.title: The Marsh at Dawn
volumes.text:
I went down to the marsh before sunrise, expecting the deepest quiet in the district. I am Ansel Corrow, a deaf old bell-ringer of Emberwick writing a study of quiet, and I thought the marsh would be my best chapter.

It was a racket. The reeds hissed. Water clucked under the boardwalk. Something boomed far off, a bittern I suppose, and every duck on the Ember had an opinion. Even my poor ears caught most of it. I stood there feeling cheated.

Then I understood that the quiet thing on the marsh was me. I had stopped walking, stopped muttering, stopped thinking about breakfast. All that noise had been there every morning of my life, and I had been too loud inside to hear it. Quiet is not always found in a place. Sometimes it is a thing the listener does.

volumes.title: The Stopped Clock
volumes.text:
My kitchen clock stopped on Tuesday night, and on Wednesday morning the room felt as if a person had left it. I, Ansel Corrow of Emberwick, had not heard that tick for years. I only heard it stop.

The sounds we live with become a floor we walk on without looking. Take the floor away and for a moment there is a drop.

I left the clock unwound for a day, on purpose, to learn what was underneath. There was a good deal. The beams of the house settling. A mouse, or the idea of a mouse. My own breath, which I am glad to report continues. I wound the clock at dusk and had to sit closer than last winter to catch it. My hearing goes on going. But I know now that under every sound there is another, smaller one.

volumes.title: Two Chairs
volumes.text:
Hob Tansley came to my door on Sunday with a jar of his pickled walnuts and no speech prepared. We had not spoken for a month, over a spoiled peal at a wedding. I, Ansel Corrow, had a speech prepared, and forgot it.

He sat in the other chair. I put a log on. Neither of us mentioned the wedding. Neither of us mentioned anything. We sat for an hour, two old ringers with our boots to the fire, and the only remark was Hob's, that the walnuts wanted another month.

It was the same silence we had kept in Emberwick market all those weeks, with not a word different. Yet that one was a wall and this one was a roof. I cannot find the difference in the quiet itself. It must lie in whether the two people are facing the same way.

volumes.title: The Bell at Rest
volumes.text:
I climbed the tower today, sixty-one steps, slower than I used. I, Ansel Corrow, rang the tenor bell of Emberwick for forty years and never once came up simply to look at her.

She hangs mouth down in the dusk of the bell chamber, as wide as a cart wheel, perfectly still. It struck me that a bell spends nearly her whole life like this. An hour's ringing on a Sunday, a wedding, a funeral, the New Year. All the rest is hanging quiet in the dark.

And that is what makes her worth hearing. A bell that rang all day would be a nuisance, and by the second week nobody would notice it. Her quiet is not time wasted between strokes. It is what the strokes are made out of. I laid my hand flat on her side. Cold, and faintly humming, from the wind.

volumes.title: What I No Longer Hear
volumes.text:
An honest account, from Ansel Corrow, once bell-ringer of Emberwick, a year into going deaf. I have lost the wren in the hedge. I have lost the treble bell entirely. I can no longer hear rain unless it means it.

What is left: the tenor bell, which I feel in my chest. Hob's laugh. The kettle's rumble, though not its singing. A door shut by someone in a temper. The clock, if I sit by it.

A year ago I should have written the first list and wept over it. I find I am more interested in the second. Each thing on it has become particular. I used to hear everything and attend to almost none of it. Now I hear little and miss none of that little. I do not call it a fair exchange. It is not nothing.

volumes.title: Room
volumes.text:
I have studied quiet for a year, in my house, on the marsh, in the library and up the bell tower, and I, Ansel Corrow, will say plainly what I think it is. Quiet is room.

It is the room the guests leave behind them, and the room the snow falls into. It is the room under the kettle's lid, and between two old friends, and around a bell. Nothing in it is missing. Something is being made space for.

So I am no longer afraid of what is coming to my ears. I am being given more room than most, and had better furnish it with attention. This evening I sat with my hand on the kettle to feel it boil. Across Emberwick the young ringers started up. I got only the tenor, one deep note in eight. It was enough to tell the tune by.

volumes.title: The Oak Log
volumes.text:
On the first Thursday of the frost, Osric Thane, retired schoolmaster of Emberwick, carried an oak log the size of a small pig into Bryony Hask's kitchen. They had agreed to share one fire a week through the winter, wood being dear.

"That is too good for an ordinary night," said Bryony, who is a weaver and knows the worth of things. "We will burn it the evening we two agree about something. Fully agree." Osric said that might be never. She said then it would keep.

They lit sticks instead. "Is this the same fire we had last year?" Osric asked. "Different wood, different flames. A new fire." Bryony said it was the same hearth and the same two fools in front of it. A fire is something that happens, like supper, and you may have supper every night. He did not agree. The log stayed in its corner.

volumes.title: Bryony's Loom
volumes.text:
Thursday again, and Osric Thane sat by Bryony Hask's fire in Emberwick, watching her mend a treadle on her loom.

"Your mother's loom," he said. "Was," said Bryony. "Or is. I've replaced the treadles twice, the beam once and every heddle." Osric, who taught school for forty years and likes a thing settled, said it was plainly a different loom, then. There was not a splinter of her mother's left in it.

Bryony tied off her cord. "There has been cloth on this loom every day since before I was born. My mother started a length and I finished it. The loom is not the wood. The loom is the going on." Osric said nobody could sit at a going on. She told him to try sitting at a pile of old treadles. The oak log they are saving for the night they agree stayed in its corner.

volumes.title: A Promise to a Dog
volumes.text:
Osric Thane came late to Bryony Hask's fire, with mud to the knee. It was their Thursday evening in Emberwick, and he had walked first to the weir and back, in the dark, with his old dog Bracken.

"I told him this morning we would go," he said. "Then it rained all day." Bryony, turning the heel of a stocking, asked whether the dog would have known. "Not in the least. He forgets a promise before I finish making it." "Then who were you keeping it for?"

Osric thought about that through one whole log. A promise has two ends, he said at last, and he was holding one of them whether or not anybody held the other. Bryony said that was only pride with wet boots. A promise nobody remembers is a plan, and plans may change with the weather. Bracken, asleep on the hearth, gave no ruling.

volumes.title: The Locked Gate
volumes.text:
"The orchard gate on Hollow Lane was locked today," said Bryony Hask, shaking snow off her shawl at Osric Thane's hearth. It was his turn to keep their Thursday fire. "Chain and padlock. No notice."

Osric asked what she had done. "Climbed it. I have walked through that orchard for thirty years. If someone wants me out they can say so. A lock doesn't say no. It doesn't say anything."

Osric said a lock says no as clearly as iron can. One does not need it in writing. Bryony replied that it might be keeping pigs in, and not weavers out. A lock is only a fact, and it is we who make it a message. He said that sounded like something a person says from the far side of a gate. In Emberwick they are saving an oak log for the night they agree. It was not tonight.

volumes.title: The Salt in the Soup
volumes.text:
Bryony Hask made leek soup for the Thursday fire, and Osric Thane, her guest and old friend, ate two bowls and said it was very good.

"It was oversalted," said Bryony. "I knocked the jar. You drank three cups of water." Osric admitted it. He had only meant to be kind. A small untruth, between friends, was a sort of cushion.

"I still have salty soup," said Bryony. "Now I also have a friend whose praise I can't spend, since I don't know which coin is good. Tell me it's salty, and then when you say a thing is fine I shall know it." Osric said that by that rule he must also tell her about the blue shawl. She said he might try. He looked at the shawl, and at the weaver who made it, and said the soup was salty. She said that would do for one evening.

volumes.title: Where the Cold Comes In
volumes.text:
Midwinter, and the wind off the Northern Fells found every crack in Osric Thane's cottage. He and Bryony Hask sat almost in the hearth for their Thursday fire. She put her hand to the bottom of the door.

"The cold is coming in here," she said. Osric, a schoolmaster to the bone, said that nothing was coming in. Cold is not a thing. There is only warmth, and the lack of it. What she felt was their heat going out.

"I have felt it come in," said Bryony. "It came across the floor and took hold of my ankle like a hand. Don't tell me that was a lack." Osric said dark was the same: no one pours dark into a room. Bryony said anyone who lay awake at three in the morning knew better. They stuffed the gap with a rolled rug, each for a different reason.

volumes.title: The Forgotten Name
volumes.text:
Osric Thane was low at Thursday's fire. A grown man had greeted him in Emberwick market that morning, as an old pupil, and Osric could not find his name. "Forty years of children," he said to Bryony Hask. "I have forgotten half of them. If I have lost half my life, am I the man who lived it?"

Bryony counted stitches before answering. "That was Ned Gurney's boy, Silas. You kept him in for drawing boats in his copybook, and then you pinned the best boat on the wall."

"I don't remember it." "No. He does. I do, now." A person is not kept all in one head, she said, like money in one pocket. Bits of Osric were lodged all over the town, in people he had forgotten. He said that was a comfort but not an answer. She said he might have the comfort meanwhile.

volumes.title: Enough Wood
volumes.text:
By February Osric Thane had counted his woodpile. "Sixty-three logs," he told Bryony Hask, at their Thursday fire in his cottage. "Four a night until the end of March, with some to spare. That is enough."

Bryony put on a fifth. He winced. "Enough is not a number," she said. "Enough is when I stop being cold. Some nights that's two logs and some nights seven." Osric said that people who burn by feeling end in April sitting in their coats. She said that people who burn by counting sit in their coats all winter and have logs left over for the summer.

He said a careful man is never caught short. She said he was never caught warm either. Then they both looked at the corner, where the great oak log waits for the night they agree on something. Neither of them had ever counted that one in.

volumes.title: The Last Slice
volumes.text:
There was one slice of ginger cake left on the plate at Bryony Hask's fire, and two people. "You cut and I choose," said Osric Thane. "That is how fairness is taught in every schoolroom in Emberwick. Two equal halves."

Bryony held the knife and did not cut. "You walked to the Grey Coast road and back today. I sat at a loom. Is equal fair?" Osric said equal was the only fair that could be measured. Once you begin weighing who is hungrier and who deserves, there is no end to it, and the cake goes stale.

"It ends when both of us think it's right," said Bryony. She cut the slice two-thirds and one-third and pushed the larger at him. He said he could not accept it. She said then he must explain why his fairness left him unhappy with more cake. He ate it, frowning.

volumes.title: The Riveted Cup
volumes.text:
Osric Thane dropped Bryony Hask's blue cup on her hearthstone, at their Thursday fire, and it broke in two. He was more upset than she was. The next week he brought it back from the tinker in Emberwick market, joined with three brass rivets.

"It will never be what it was," he said. "A mended thing is a spoiled thing made the best of." Bryony turned it in the firelight. She said she liked it better. Before, it was one of six. Now it was the cup Osric broke the winter they shared a fire, and she would know it in the dark.

"It leaks a little," he said. "So do you," said Bryony, "and nobody thinks of throwing you out." He held that whole is still better than mended, if one is honest. She held that whole is only what a thing is before anything has happened to it.

volumes.title: What Talking Is For
volumes.text:
"Eleven weeks," said Osric Thane, by Bryony Hask's fire, "and we have not agreed once. Not on fires, looms, dogs, gates, soup, cold, cake or cups." He nodded at the corner of her Emberwick kitchen, where the oak log they had saved for the night of agreement sat with the cat asleep on it. "Talk that settles nothing is a road that goes nowhere."

"I walk to the weir most mornings," said Bryony. "I don't go there to be at the weir. There's nothing at the weir. I go for the going."

Osric opened his mouth to say she was right, and saw the log. If he agreed, they must burn it, and the cat would lose her seat, and the winter would be over. He shut his mouth. Bryony saw him do it, and laughed, and said nothing either.

volumes.title: The Log Burns
volumes.text:
The last Thursday of the winter was mild. There were crocuses by Bryony Hask's gate in Emberwick and the door stood open. She and Osric Thane hardly needed a fire, but they lit a small one from habit and sat looking at the oak log in the corner, saved since the first frost for the evening they should fully agree.

"I have been thinking," said Osric, "that the best of these evenings were the ones when we got nowhere." Bryony said she had thought so since November. "Then we agree," said Osric, and looked alarmed.

They lifted the log on together. It caught slowly and burned until past midnight, and they sat by it with nothing left to settle. At the door he said he would bring another oak log at the first frost. Bryony said he might, and that she expected to find something wrong with it.

volumes.title: Noon: The Charge
volumes.text:
My brother-in-law Edwin said on Sunday, meaning no harm, that since I gave up the post office my afternoons must be all alike. I, Lettice Marrow, have been cross about it for two days. Today I mean to be useful about it instead.

I shall examine one afternoon. This one, the tenth of October, in Emberwick, with nothing arranged. I shall watch it from the stroke of noon until I light the lamp, and write down what is in it, a notebook to each half hour if need be. If it is empty, Edwin is right and I shall say so.

The clock has just struck twelve. Before I begin I have written what I expect: dinner, a letter, a walk to the post, tea. Four things. It looks a thin list, I admit. The cat is on the windowsill and the sun has reached the second flagstone. I begin.

volumes.title: Bread and Cheese
volumes.text:
Half past twelve on the tenth of October, the afternoon I, Lettice Marrow of Emberwick, have set myself to examine. Dinner is bread, cheese and an apple, as it is most days. My brother-in-law would say: there, all alike.

But I walked to the baker's this morning and I am hungry, and the bread tastes better than it did on Sunday when I was not. So I put a question to my plate. Is the pleasure in the bread or in the hunger?

I ate the first slice quickly and the second slowly. The second was better, though cut from the same loaf. So some of it is neither bread nor hunger, but attention. That makes three things on the plate where I expected one. I have kept the apple for later, to see whether waiting improves it.

volumes.title: One Plate
volumes.text:
One o'clock. I, Lettice Marrow, am examining this single afternoon in my kitchen in Emberwick, and it has brought me to the washing-up, which is one plate, one knife and a cup.

I have always called this a chore, by which I meant time that does not count. Today I watched it. The water was warm. The plate, which was my mother's, has a blue rim worn pale where forty years of thumbs have held it. I dried it and it squeaked.

It took four minutes. I cannot see what was wrong with those four minutes. They were not waiting for something else. If I throw out every hour I have called a chore, I throw out a third of my life with the dishwater. The plate is clean, and I made it so. That is a small thing to have done by one o'clock, but it is done.

volumes.title: The Unanswered Letter
volumes.text:
Half past one, on the afternoon I have promised to examine honestly. Honesty brings me to the mantelpiece, where a letter from my cousin Dorothea in the Lowlands has stood for three weeks, looking at me.

I want to have answered it. I do not want to answer it. I, Lettice Marrow, sorted the letters of Emberwick for thirty years and never understood this about them: the reply grows heavier each day it is not written, though the paper weighs the same.

So I sat down and wrote only the first line. "Dear Dorothea, I am ashamed to be so late." And there the weight went. It had all been in that one line. The rest ran on by itself, two sides and a postscript. I think most of what I put off is like that. The task is small. The door to it is stiff.

volumes.title: The Nap Not Examined
volumes.text:
Two o'clock. I must report a gap. I, Lettice Marrow, who set out to examine every minute of this October afternoon in Emberwick, sat down in the chair by the window with the sun on my lap, to rest my eyes for a moment.

The clock now says a quarter past. The cat has moved from the sill to my knee without my leave. I have no account of those minutes whatever.

The room went on without me. The sun moved a hand's breadth along the floor. I was the only thing in it not attending. I could pretend I was thinking, and nobody would know. But the record must be honest or it is no use. So: a quarter of an hour, unexamined, and I feel the better for it. Perhaps an afternoon needs one room that is kept locked.

volumes.title: The Third Door
volumes.text:
Half past two, and I am walking down Hollow Lane to the post box by the bridge. I, Lettice Marrow, carried the Emberwick post along this lane for thirty years. Today I am examining my afternoon, so I tried examining the lane.

I set myself a test. Without looking, what colour is the third door? Green, I guessed. It is blue, with a brass fish for a knocker. I must have knocked that fish a thousand times.

What we know best, it seems, we see least. I knew the lane so well that I had stopped looking, and had been walking through my own idea of it. So I looked. There is a pear tree trained against the fifth house. There is a boot scraper shaped like a hedgehog. The lane was full of things, and all of them had been there on every one of my alike afternoons.

volumes.title: The Stranger's Question
volumes.text:
Three o'clock by the bridge clock, on the afternoon I am examining. A carter stopped me, a stranger, and asked the way to the Grey Coast road. I, Lettice Marrow, told him: over the bridge, left at the smithy, straight on. He thanked me and drove off.

I had gone twenty paces when I doubted. Left at the smithy, or right? I have known that turning all my life, and the moment someone depended on it, it wobbled.

He was nobody to me. If he went wrong he would lose half an hour and think poorly of an old woman in Emberwick. And yet I turned and ran, at my age, with my hat in my hand, and caught him at the bridge end to say it again. It was left. It had been left all along. I do not know what I owed him, but my legs knew.

volumes.title: A Bench by the Ember
volumes.text:
Half past three. Having run after a carter, I, Lettice Marrow, sat down on the bench below the bridge to get my breath. I am examining one whole afternoon in Emberwick, and here was a stretch with nothing in it. I decided to do nothing, properly, and see what that is like.

It cannot be done. I sat still, and found I was watching a yellow leaf come down the river. It turned twice, caught on a stone, thought it over, and went on under the arch. Then I was listening to the weir. Then I was wondering who first put a bench here.

So doing nothing is only doing something small enough to be overlooked. I sat a quarter of an hour, and it was as full as any other quarter this afternoon. I begin to suspect there is no such thing as an empty one.

volumes.title: The Child at the Gate
volumes.text:
Four o'clock. At my own gate I, Lettice Marrow, met Tam from next door, who is six, swinging on it. I told him I was examining my afternoon. He asked when the afternoon stops.

I said at evening. He asked when that was. I said when it gets dark. He pointed out, fairly, that it gets dark slowly, and wanted to know which minute. I had no minute to give him. The sky over Emberwick was plainly still afternoon. In two hours it would plainly be evening, and I should never catch it changing.

Tam thought this a poor answer from a grown person. But I have turned it over since. There is no line, and yet the two sides are different. Most things I am sure of are like that: young and old, enough and too much. I gave him the apple I had saved from dinner.

volumes.title: The Watched Kettle
volumes.text:
Half past four, and tea. I, Lettice Marrow, have been watching my afternoon since noon, as an experiment, and now I am watching the kettle, and it will not boil.

Everyone knows this about kettles. I had not thought what it means. The kettle takes the same time whether I look or not. It is the time that changes: watched, it stretches. And I have watched this whole afternoon, which is why it is only half past four and I feel I have lived a week since dinner.

So perhaps my afternoons seemed alike, and short, because I never looked at them. I let them boil behind my back. I should not care to watch every kettle of my life. But it is something to know that an afternoon is as long as I choose to make it. The lid has begun to rattle. I shall use the good cup.

volumes.title: The Light Going
volumes.text:
Five o'clock. The sun has left the flagstones and climbed the far wall of my kitchen, where it has turned the whitewash the colour of the inside of a shell. I, Lettice Marrow, have examined this afternoon since noon, and now it is going.

I tried to catch the moment when I should need the lamp. I could read my own writing. I could still read it. Then I found I had been holding the page to the window for some time. The moment had gone by without telling me.

I did not expect to mind. But this was the tenth of October, with a blue door in it, and a carter, and a leaf, and it will not come again. Tomorrow will have other things in it. Whatever my brother-in-law Edwin thinks, my afternoons were never alike. I only failed to tell them apart.

volumes.title: Lamp-Lighting
volumes.text:
I have lit the lamp, and by my own rule the afternoon is over. I, Lettice Marrow, set out at noon to examine one ordinary afternoon in Emberwick, because my brother-in-law Edwin said mine were all the same.

I expected four things: dinner, a letter, a walk, tea. I have filled eleven notebooks, and this is the twelfth. There was bread that changed with attention, a plate, a stiff door, a gap, a blue door, a stranger, a leaf, a child's question, a kettle, a wall the colour of a shell.

So here is my answer, Edwin. My afternoons look alike from outside, as the books on a library shelf look alike with their covers shut. I shall not examine tomorrow's. One need not read every book to know they are full. I am sending you the twelve notebooks by the morning post, tied with string. The label says: "Tuesday."

volumes.title: The Barley-Sugar Jar
volumes.text:
I am Ida Fennimore, and I have taught the lower school at Emberwick for nineteen years without once being asked a thing I could not answer, or at least answer firmly. Then Wren Ashby turned nine.

On Monday I blew out the candle after the early lesson, and Wren put up her hand. "Where does the flame go?" I said it goes out. "Out where?" I said it simply stops. She asked how a thing can stop without going anywhere, since when she stops she is still standing there.

Eleven faces waited. I said we would come back to it, which is what teachers say. After school I wrote the question on a slip, put it in an empty barley-sugar jar, and put the jar at the back of my desk drawer, meaning to look the answer up. A teacher ought to know. I shut the drawer rather quickly.

volumes.title: Your Blue and Mine
volumes.text:
A second slip has gone into the jar in my desk, where I, Ida Fennimore, schoolmistress of Emberwick, keep the questions I cannot answer. Wren Ashby again. She is nine.

We were painting bluebells. Wren looked at her neighbour Tam's paper and asked: "When I see blue, and Tam sees blue, how do we know it's the same?" I said we both call it blue. She said yes, but suppose what Tam sees is what she would call yellow, and he calls it blue because everyone told him to.

We matched the bluebell to the sky, to my shawl, to the inkwell. Tam and Wren agreed every time, which proved nothing. Nobody can climb in behind another person's eyes to look. All we have is that we point at the same things and say the same word. Wren thought that was not much. I think it may be nearly everything.

volumes.title: How Long Is Now
volumes.text:
This one came during arithmetic, which is when Wren Ashby does her best thinking about other things. I am her teacher, Ida Fennimore, and I keep a jar in my desk at Emberwick school for her questions that I cannot answer. "Miss, when you say now, how long is it?"

I said now is this moment. She asked how long a moment is. A minute is plainly too long; its beginning is already then by the time you reach its end. We listened to the school clock. Even a tick has a front and a back.

Wren clapped her hands once and said "now", and we agreed that by the time we heard it, it was over. So now is too short to hold anything, and yet everything that ever happens to us happens in it. I wrote the slip. The class clapped for some minutes more, to make sure.

volumes.title: A Heap of Peas
volumes.text:
We were counting dried peas, the lower school and I, Ida Fennimore, on a wet morning in Emberwick. I tipped the bag out on the table and said, "Here is a heap." That was my mistake. Wren Ashby, who is nine and asks questions I cannot answer, took one pea away.

"Still a heap?" Yes. She took another. Still a heap. She went on, pea by pea, and the class watched as if at a play. At last there were three peas in a row, and nobody would call that a heap. But nobody could say which pea had done it.

No single pea makes the difference, and yet the difference gets made. I wrote that on a slip for the jar in my desk. Then we put the peas back, one at a time, to see where the heap began. We could not find that either.

volumes.title: Before the First Day
volumes.text:
"What was the day before the first day?" asked Wren Ashby, who is nine. This time I, Ida Fennimore, took the barley-sugar jar of unanswered questions out of my desk and carried it, after school, to Emberwick Library.

I sat at the long table until the lamp was lit in the window. The books were interesting, and did not agree. On the day before the first day, three of them said three different things, and the fourth said the question should not be asked.

Next morning I stood before the class and said, "I do not know. And the books do not know either." I had expected to feel smaller. Instead eleven children leaned forward, as they never do for the rivers of the Lowlands. Wren looked at me as if I had finally said something sensible. I put the jar back in the drawer, but not at the back.

volumes.title: The Cat's Dream
volumes.text:
The school cat at Emberwick is called Inkpot, and she sleeps on the windowsill through every lesson I, Ida Fennimore, have ever given. On Thursday her paws began to twitch. Wren Ashby, aged nine, my most difficult pupil in the best sense, put her hand up.

"Is she dreaming? What about?" Mice, said the class. Wren said we didn't know that. It might be fish. It might be us. It might not be pictures at all, since a cat knows the world mostly by smell.

We cannot ask Inkpot. And Wren went one further: we cannot really ask each other. When Tam says he dreamed of falling, we take his word and imagine our own falling. I said that taking each other's word is what a school is for. The slip went into my jar of questions without answers. Inkpot woke, washed, and told us nothing.

volumes.title: Where the Hole Goes
volumes.text:
On Friday the baker sent ring cakes to Emberwick school, the kind with a hole in the middle, and I, Ida Fennimore, should have known better than to hand one to Wren Ashby. She is nine. I keep a jar of her questions that have no answers.

She looked at me through it. "When I eat the cake, where does the hole go?" The class said it gets eaten. Wren said nobody can eat a hole. You can count holes. You can fall in one. But you cannot take one home without bringing the cake.

I said a hole is perhaps a thing that belongs to something else, like a shadow, or a birthday. Wren considered this and ate the cake in a circle, slowly, watching. At the last bite she said, "It was there, and I didn't see it go." Another slip for the jar.

volumes.title: Why I Am Me
volumes.text:
It was a still afternoon at Emberwick school and I, Ida Fennimore, had set the lower class to copying. Wren Ashby, who is nine, stopped with her pen in the air. I know that look. I keep a jar in my desk for what follows it.

"Miss. Why am I the one who's me?" There are twelve of us in the room, she said, each looking out of their own eyes, and she is the one looking out of Wren's. Why isn't she looking out of Tam's, and worrying about Tam's lost boot?

I said if she were, she would be Tam, and asking the same thing. She said yes, that was exactly the trouble. I have explained the tides, and long division, and where the Ember rises. I had nothing. I said, "I have wondered that since I was about your age." I had forgotten it until she asked.

volumes.title: A New Colour
volumes.text:
For a week Wren Ashby has been trying to think of a colour nobody has seen. She is nine, and my pupil at Emberwick school, and when I, Ida Fennimore, told the class that people can imagine anything, she took it as a wager.

Monday's colour turned out to be a sort of green. Tuesday's was purple with the light behind it. On Wednesday she had a real one, she said, but could only tell me what it was not.

By Friday she was indignant. "I can't. I can only stir up the ones I've got." I tried it myself at home, with my eyes shut, for longer than I shall admit. The mind, it seems, is a paintbox and not a paint factory. Yet somebody must once have seen blue for the first time. It is in the jar where I keep the questions I cannot answer.

volumes.title: Where the Word Went
volumes.text:
On Tuesday Wren Ashby, who is nine, could not remember the word thimble. She was telling the class at Emberwick school about her grandmother's sewing, and stopped. "The little hat for your finger." We all knew it. I, Ida Fennimore, her teacher, held my tongue, because she shook her head at us. She wanted to find it herself.

It came back at supper, she told me next day, while she was thinking about gravy. "So where was it?" It had never left her head. Yet she had looked everywhere in there.

I said perhaps it was like a thing fallen behind a dresser. She asked who moves the dresser. I do not know who moves the dresser. I have lost names and found them all my life and never asked where they spend the afternoon. My jar of questions without answers is nearly full.

volumes.title: The Jar on the Desk
volumes.text:
Wren Ashby stayed behind today to help me, Ida Fennimore, wash the inkwells at Emberwick school. She is nine, and goes up to the big school over the bridge after the summer. Looking for a cloth, she opened my desk drawer and found a barley-sugar jar packed with paper slips.

She knew her own questions at once. Where the flame goes. Whether her blue is mine. "You kept them. Why didn't you answer them?" I said I could not. "Not any?" Not one.

She looked at the jar, and then at my shelf, where the book of answers for arithmetic stands, which is thin. "Are there more questions than answers, Miss?" I said I had begun to think so, and that a year ago it would have frightened me. She said it sounded like more to do. I stood the jar on top of the desk, in the light.

volumes.title: The Lid Left Off
volumes.text:
On the last day of term I, Ida Fennimore, wrote a slip of my own for the jar of unanswered questions on my desk at Emberwick school. "What should a teacher do with a question she cannot answer?"

I held it over the jar and could not put it in. It has an answer. I have been doing it all year. You keep the question. You say you do not know. You ask it again, with company.

Wren Ashby, who filled that jar, left at four for the big school over the bridge. She gave me a slip, folded small: "Who will ask you things now?" I stood the jar on the windowsill with the lid off and a pencil on a string. On the first morning of next term, before I had my coat off, there was a slip in it, in large letters. "Why is the jar full?"
